name: Squall-Basin
description: Squall-Basin is a small oceanic world dominated by a single supercontinent-sized depression in the ocean floor, a basin so vast it creates its own tidal and weather patterns. Sudden squalls erupt without warning across the basin's surface, churning the otherwise placid waters into brief, violent storms that dissipate as quickly as they form. The sky is a watercolor wash of blues and whites, with cloud formations cycling through their entire lifecycle in under an hour.

The rapid weather cycles give Squall-Basin a frenetic energy that contrasts with its serene appearance from orbit. One moment the surface is glass-calm and reflective, the next it is a howling wall of spray and wind. The geothermal vents along the basin floor warm the deep water, and the resulting convection currents drive the unpredictable surface weather. The air smells of salt and sulfur in equal measure.

Despite its dynamic surface, Squall-Basin harbors only microbial life, though in staggering variety and density. The geothermal vent communities represent some of the most complex microbial ecosystems ever documented, with thousands of species occupying micro-niches in the mineral chimneys. Xenobiologists believe the world is in a pre-Cambrian stage of development, with complex multicellular life potentially millions of years away.

Squall-Basin offers a rare window into the earliest stages of biological evolution on an oceanic world. The helium-3 dissolved in its waters provides economic incentive for a permanent presence, but the unpredictable squalls make surface operations hazardous. Submersible research is safer but expensive, and there is growing debate about whether resource extraction might disrupt the delicate microbial ecosystems before they have a chance to evolve further.
